articles.description: There is very little on which the National Post and the Toronto Star can agree in this age of polarization. As bastions of the right and the left in Canadian media, they squabble over the environment, women’s rights and race. But on one thing they seem to agree: masculinity is in crisis. The National Post complains that “plenty of commentators claim the manosphere is luring boys into monstrous ideas.” The Toronto Star argues that “young men don’t benefit from what the right is selling them.” The two newspapers reach opposite conclusions, but they start from the same premise: that there is a normative masculinity, that it is now in crisis and that their readers share an understanding of what “crisis” means. That shared understanding is rarely examined. Media portrayals of the “crisis of masculinity” seldom ask what is actually meant when the words “crisis” and “masculinity” are invoked. Asking those questions reveals two things: when, and for whom, the crisis label gets applied is heavily unequal. And the “masculinity” said to be in crisis is often a very specific, very white kind of masculinity. What is a crisis? “Crisis” comes from the Greek krinō , which meant merely a decisive moment and the reaching of a verdict about said moment. Around the 18th century, as historian and theorist Reinhart Koselleck notes , crisis came to be associated with a new kind of temporality: no longer just the moment of decision, but the time after it — the end of the era in which the decision was made. Any crisis, then, contains a tacit agreement between whoever declares it — a politician, an advocate, a newspaper — and the people being told about it. Both must accept that there is a state of normalcy against which the crisis is defined. But as anthropologist Janet Roitman points out , what is and is not normative is socially constructed. There is no empirical state of “crisis” or “non-crisis.” A crisis is perhaps best understood, then, as a social label applied to a series of failures of category, in this case gender. In its current usage, a crisis is a failure mediated through political and ideological frameworks . It becomes a crisis when someone says it is, and when the failure is taken as a symptom of a wider problem. Crisis as a political tool The right’s embrace of crisis rhetoric has been studied by the likes of political scientist Benjamin Moffitt. In his 2015 paper “How to Perform Crisis: A Model for Understanding the Key Role of Crisis in Contemporary Populism,” he describes “crisis” as an “ill-defined” yet politically salient category. It’s one that far-right populists such as Geert Wilders, leader of the Netherlands’ Party for Freedom , and Australia’s Pauline Hanson, leader of the One Nation party , mobilize to rally their bases. The political right has raised the profile of the “crisis of masculinity” over the past decade, and the frame has travelled. In a November 2025 interview on CNN’s State of the Union , California Gov. Gavin Newsom lamented that, in his view, Democrats had ceded ground on the “crisis of masculinity” by not taking the epidemic of male suicide seriously . When a Democratic governor adopts the phrase, it is no longer only a right-wing talking point. Which men? The “crisis of masculinity” usually refers to a wide range of problems, but it rarely specifies the kind of man on whom those problems fall. Men do die by suicide at higher rates than women in Canada (roughly three times the rate) . But those rates are far from even among men. Among Inuit in Nunavut, for example, suicide occurs at about 10 times the rate in the rest of Canada , and young men are at highest risk . Inuit have named this a crisis themselves. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami’s 2016 National Inuit Suicide Prevention Strategy frames suicide among Inuit as a preventable public health crisis that demands a systemic response. Indigenous men are also more likely than anyone else in Canada to be killed . In 2020, police reported 201 Indigenous homicide victims; 163 of them were men . That year, the homicide rate for Indigenous men was almost eight times the rate for non-Indigenous men. Government agencies have documented this harm. Yet it rarely appears when commentators talk about “the crisis of masculinity.” The people closest to the harm name the crisis long before those with power treat it as one. What becomes clear, then, is that this “crisis” is often about the grievances of white men. articles.title: The ‘crisis of masculinity’ often excludes those most at risk, including Indigenous and racialized men

articles.content: Typical cases of 'rebirth syndrome' encompass narrative, biological, emotional and behavioural components. Painting: Luke Fildes's 'The Doctor' ( Wikimedia Commons) For more than 60 years, the University of Virginia’s Division of Perceptual Studies (DOPS) has collected information about children who seemingly recall past lives. Its digitized database contains 2,254 records with more than 200 variables for each case. Most of these children provided enough detail to unambiguously identify a previous identity. Based on 1,678 matched cases (released as open data ), DOPS researchers found that an unexpected death was associated with a shorter “intermission period” before rebirth. This study has generated wide coverage in English and Spanish media . Most news outlets highlight these findings as “striking.” However, as a causal inference specialist, I think the pattern in the DOPS study might reflect something much simpler and less exciting: selection bias. Unexpected deaths are more likely to be newsworthy. News archives, in turn, are the type of source that DOPS researchers use to identify potential matches. This selection effect builds up over time and can easily explain the main study findings. The bullfighter K’s story is not part of the DOPS database, but is typical of children’s statements about past lives. I learned about it through K’s mother, Made. She shared her story online after viewing a social media reel about reincarnation. I reached out to Made because very few cases had been studied in Latin America; none in my native Ecuador. Made told me that K was three years old when he sat on his bed and spontaneously began telling Made and her husband about having lived as a bullfighter in Spain. K told them he remembered a bull stuck its horn in his stomach. “Here,” he said, lifting his T-shirt and putting his finger above the left hip, where he has a birthmark. The bull goring had caused him severe pain and he was taken to the hospital. “Then I died, and after that I woke up with you two,” Made recalls him saying. Birthmarks or birth defects are not unheard of among children who seemingly recall past lives. However, a deep emotional involvement is the key component. Made says that after explaining his death, K talked about his previous family and how much he missed them. “He had tears in his eyes when he talked about his other mum,” Made told me. Both of K’s parents were dumbfounded, as neither had ever entertained the idea that reincarnation was real. “My husband is Catholic and I am evangelical Christian,” Made says. At the time — nine years ago — the family lived in Quito, Ecuador, and neither parent had ever visited Spain. According to them, there had been no references to that country, let alone bullfighting, as they only allowed K to watch age-appropriate content. Biology and memory Biology does not provide straight answers about children who seemingly recall past lives, but the field is exploring a question relevant to it: what mechanisms allow for memory transmission outside of the brain and between generations? Biologist Michael Levin started experimenting with Planaria — flatworms with a remarkable ability to regenerate severed parts — because he wanted to know if they would retain memories in a regenerated head. These invertebrates have most of the same neurotransmitters humans do and have become an influential model for the study of the brain. Levin conducted a simple experiment that took advantage of the planaria’s proclivity to always examine unknown terrain. The results showed that the worms seemed to remember the terrain, even though Levin had chopped their entire heads off. The study suggests “that some trace of memory is stored in locations distributed beyond the brain.” Levin later suggested that researchers should look at epigenetic mechanisms (factors that influence gene expression), “but this alone doesn’t begin to explain it.” In a recent interview , DOPS researcher Philip Cozzolino shared researchers’ plans to search for epigenetic signatures in children who claim to recall a past life, particularly among those who seem to behave as if they have survived trauma. In a 2005 review of a book about children’s past life memories, Levin discussed the flatworm model in that context, noting that it “doesn’t take us all the way to a discarnate entity, and may or may not apply to higher vertebrates, but it provides a foot-hold to begin, giving biologists an experimentally tractable entry-point into the process of how information could be imposed on a forming brain from outside the brain.” In 2023, a study conducted on roundworms ( C. Elegans ) suggested that associative memories may be transferred across generations. More recently, biologist Martha R. Weiss held an online seminar about butterflies’ learning and memory. She shared the findings of her youngest-ever collaborator — 10-year-old Jo Nagai — who had just confirmed that his butterflies recalled associations they had learned as caterpillars. Then, he pushed the study further. Weiss reported that Jo “found persistence of memory into the next generation. And right now we are writing up his results for publication.” Addressing selection bias We know there are cases out there that have never been studied because people like Made didn’t approach anyone. These cases involve people who share their stories online but are not part of any database. Looking at the same social media reel that Made saw, you could see dozens of parents claiming at least some partial resemblance to the prototypical case of “ rebirth syndrome ” that encompasses narrative, biological, emotional and behavioural components. There is a straightforward way to address selection bias. Rather than waiting for families to approach researchers when a child reports a troubling memory, researchers could directly ask all families instead. Talking to a full crowd at the Behind and Beyond the Brain Symposium , which I attended in April 2026, former DOPS director Jim Tucker shared some preliminary results. They started with a convenience sample of mothers in Virginia. When Tucker looked at the numbers, the proportion was so high he thought something had gone wrong. DOPS then developed an 11-item assessment and established a threshold to make sure the measure was robust. Then, they improved the target population. Using a nationally representative sample of English-speaking mothers in the United States with children ages 5 to 13 (whom they have raised since the child was 3), DOPS researchers found that 6.9 per cent of mothers reported having the type of emotionally meaningful interaction Made had with K. The path forward Psychological research into people who claim to remember past lives has historically studied only a very small number of individuals. Not only due to stigma (you can start with the intention of disproving the phenomena ) but precisely because it was assumed the cases were extremely rare. The high prevalence of “rebirth syndrome” opens the door to population-level studies. Developmental cohorts — study designs that regularly ask parents about many aspects of a child’s life over time — could firmly establish associations between these memories and many other facets of the human psyche. DOPS, for example, found that people who recall past lives as the opposite sex are significantly more likely to display gender non-conforming traits . I look forward to the day when researchers embrace the study of the “rebirth” phenomenon (even if they ultimately attribute it to fantasy). Taking a first step could be as simple as incorporating DOPS’ 11-item assessment into their existing studies. Such a small choice could reshape not only how we understand the interplay between memory and biology, but also our understanding of where we come from, the nature of mind and the deeper questions about human existence that science has rarely had the opportunity to explore. Jorge Andrés Delgado-Ron does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57 per cent of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69 per cent of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability . According to Restaurants Canada , 41 per cent of operators are either losing money or breaking even. At the same time, restaurants face growing pressure to reduce their environmental impact. Food production uses land, water and energy, and generates greenhouse gas emissions. Animal-based products generally have a larger environmental footprint than plant-based foods . Restaurants contribute to these impacts through food purchasing, energy consumption and waste. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted globally in 2022, with food services accounting for 28 per cent. My recent review of sustainability efforts in restaurants and cafés examined 57 studies published between 2015 and 2025. The review found that relatively simple changes to menus and portions can influence what people order. These changes offer restaurants an opportunity to influence what customers eat while pursuing more sustainable operations. The challenge is implementing them in ways that customers accept and businesses can afford. The economics of going green Restaurants face rising costs on almost every front. Ninety-one per cent of operators cite food costs and 87 per cent cite labour as major pressures. Introducing new ingredients, suppliers or kitchen routines can add costs and carry risk. Restaurants must also consider whether customers will accept those changes, particularly when affordability already influences their decisions so heavily. Smaller portions could cut waste, for example, but diners may feel they’re getting less for their money. Plant-based dishes have to compete with familiar favourites on taste, price and appeal. These are all considerations that must be taken into account when restaurants design sustainability initiatives. Initiatives that customers reject or that restaurants cannot afford are unlikely to last. However, it’s important to note not every environmental improvement requires additional spending. Reducing food waste, for instance, can lower purchasing and disposal costs . How restaurants affect consumer choices Restaurants have considerable influence over what their customers eat. What’s on the menu, how dishes are described, pricing and portion sizes can all shape purchasing decisions. Research suggests modifying the food environment can be more effective than relying on consumers to make different choices on their own. In a study conducted in Dutch restaurants , doubling vegetable portions while reducing meat portions by an average of 12.5 per cent increased vegetable consumption from approximately 62 grams to 115 grams per diner, without compromising customer satisfaction. Other interventions include making healthier options easier to see, introducing them as the default, adjusting portion sizes and changing the composition of menus. Across the studies in my review, changing what restaurants offer and how they present it tended to be more effective than simply encouraging customers to choose differently. These changes, however, are not universally effective. One study found adding a price premium to meat and fish dishes didn’t increase vegetarian orders and made diners less interested in the menu. In another example , removing all meat burgers sharply reduced customer satisfaction. Communication also matters. Labelling dishes as meat-free can discourage some regular meat eaters, particularly when the messaging feels preachy. On the other hand, appealing, neutral descriptions have shown to have more promising results. Balancing profit and sustainability There is also evidence menu changes can deliver commercial benefits. Research combining multiple strategies , including adding healthier options, improving menu displays and offering lower-priced meal combinations, increased sales of healthier items without reducing overall revenue. However, increased sales of particular dishes do not necessarily translate into reduced environmental impacts. A restaurant might sell more plant-based meals without knowing whether its environmental footprint has actually dropped. Similarly, smaller portions only reduce food waste if less food is actually discarded. My review highlights the need to evaluate these outcomes together. Only 10 per cent of the studies in my review directly measured environmental outcomes, primarily food waste. None measured greenhouse gas emissions, resource consumption or broader environmental impacts. Although 40 per cent examined financial outcomes such as sales and orders, these measures did not necessarily establish whether interventions were profitable. Just 10 per cent included follow-up assessments beyond the immediate intervention period. The evidence points to promising approaches, but more comprehensive evaluation is needed to establish which interventions deliver the greatest environmental and commercial returns. What needs to change Restaurants should prioritize interventions that are both operationally practical and commercially viable. Involving both owners and managers in designing changes can help ensure they reflect the realities of purchasing, food preparation and customer expectations. Studies involving restaurant stakeholders found that this approach made changes more practical and acceptable. . Low-cost options offer a starting point. Adjusting portions to reduce uneaten food, using appealing dish names, making plant-based dishes easier to find and reducing food waste were among the most promising strategies identified in my review. Restaurants should also track food waste, ingredient costs, sales and customer responses to determine which changes deliver results. Ultimately, sustainable dining depends on reducing environmental impacts while maintaining customer satisfaction and commercial viability. Sadaf Mollaei receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC) (Grant number: 430958), University of Guelph, and the Arrell Food Institute for funding this project.

articles.content: At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, a key question for negotiators is how to get more money to developing countries so they can adapt to a warming world. For the past 30 years, climate talks focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions and preventing future global warming. However, the United Nations now expects global warming to exceed the 1.5 C target outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement. That could bring greater risks of drought, flooding, rising seas and wildfires in the future. Countries now have little choice but to adapt to a warming planet. The host country sees carbon markets as part of the answer. These markets allow countries or companies that emit greenhouse gases to buy credits that pay for projects that reduce emissions elsewhere. These often include projects that plant or protect trees or change farming practices. Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, who is leading the summit, says carbon markets could raise more than US$50 billion a year in extra finance for developing countries by 2030. I have studied carbon markets on farms and in forests for two decades, including fieldwork on carbon projects in India, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania and Vietnam. In one of my first papers , in 2006, my colleagues and I cautioned that such projects could leave out poor farmers and those without formal land titles. Low carbon prices and the high cost of signing up many small farms would also make it hard for smallholders to benefit. Many of those concerns remain unresolved. This matters because countries are being asked to put far more money into adaptation, much of it on farms and in forests. Raising money is difficult, and as a 2023 working paper I co-authored shows , designing carbon projects that work, and measuring their impact, is even more difficult. Adaptation is no longer optional Part of the Thar Desert in western Rajasthan, India. Communities here already face extreme heatwaves and need support to adapt their farming and herding livelihoods to changing conditions. (Rohit Jindal) , CC BY-NC-ND Developing countries need about US$305 billion a year to adapt, roughly 10 times the US$28 billion in international support they received in 2024. Last year, countries called for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035. They also agreed on 59 indicators to track progress . Eleven of these relate to food production and ecosystems, including farms and forests. Many of the practices involved, like improving soils, planting trees and protecting forests, are similar to what carbon markets have tried to promote. Hopes like Kurum’s are not new, but carbon markets have grown slowly. In 2006, the voluntary carbon market was worth about US$90 million . By 2024, it was worth US$535 million . That year, buyers used about 70 million carbon credits from farm and forest projects, each representing one ton of carbon dioxide cut or stored. This is less than one per cent of the eight to 14 billion tons that farms and forests could deliver each year . Barriers to growing carbon markets My recently published paper , as well as research currently under peer review, identify three recurring barriers. First, it’s difficult to show that a project made a real difference. Would the forest be conserved, or would the farmer have changed practices anyway? A large study found that fewer than one in six carbon credits reflected genuine emission cuts. Second, measuring carbon in soils and trees is costly, and those costs reduce returns for farmers. In Mozambique, my colleagues and I found that a community carbon project raised household incomes only slightly , despite generous contract terms. Third, projects tend to go where they are easiest to run. China, India and Brazil hosted more than three-quarters of all projects under the UN’s original carbon credit scheme. In Africa, we found as early as 2008 that insecure land rights discouraged new investment . Climate change is also affecting projects themselves. In Tanzania’s Uluguru Mountains, my colleagues and I offered farmers contracts to plant and protect trees in 2009. Twenty-one months later, 63 per cent of the trees had survived , with some losses linked to the failure of the short rains. Adaptation projects are likely to face all of these barriers, and more. Carbon projects measure their success in a single unit, tons of carbon dioxide, which can be turned into credits and sold. Adaptation has no such common measure. Success might mean less damage from a flood, or harvests that survive a drought. Such benefits can take years to appear and are hard to measure. What would help? Three lessons from carbon markets stand out. Keep measurement simple and local. In field experiments in Vietnam, my colleagues and I found that villagers rarely cheated when monitoring their own work , so communities can help check results themselves. Lower the cost of implementation and make sure funds reach farmers. Carbon projects must pay to find buyers, negotiate contracts, receive government approval and hire independent auditors before earning any money. Governments and international organizations can help cut these upfront costs by simplifying rules and making it easier to work with community groups that can sign up many farmers at once. Directing support to places most at risk, not only those where projects are easier to set up. Small pilots can help countries learn what works. More money for adaptation is badly needed. But without credible projects on the ground, that money will struggle to make a difference. articles.description: At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, a key question for negotiators is how to get more money to developing countries so they can adapt to a warming world. For the past 30 years, climate talks focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions and preventing future global warming. However, the United Nations now expects global warming to exceed the 1.5 C target outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement. That could bring greater risks of drought, flooding, rising seas and wildfires in the future. Countries now have little choice but to adapt to a warming planet. The host country sees carbon markets as part of the answer. These markets allow countries or companies that emit greenhouse gases to buy credits that pay for projects that reduce emissions elsewhere. These often include projects that plant or protect trees or change farming practices. Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, who is leading the summit, says carbon markets could raise more than US$50 billion a year in extra finance for developing countries by 2030. I have studied carbon markets on farms and in forests for two decades, including fieldwork on carbon projects in India, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania and Vietnam. In one of my first papers , in 2006, my colleagues and I cautioned that such projects could leave out poor farmers and those without formal land titles. Low carbon prices and the high cost of signing up many small farms would also make it hard for smallholders to benefit. Many of those concerns remain unresolved. This matters because countries are being asked to put far more money into adaptation, much of it on farms and in forests. Raising money is difficult, and as a 2023 working paper I co-authored shows , designing carbon projects that work, and measuring their impact, is even more difficult. Adaptation is no longer optional Part of the Thar Desert in western Rajasthan, India. Communities here already face extreme heatwaves and need support to adapt their farming and herding livelihoods to changing conditions. articles.content: By supporting young children's emerging understanding of number, we can help them develop strong foundations to support their later mathematics learning. (Pixabay) As adults, we may take for granted what we know about numbers and how we arrived at this knowledge — for example, when comparing item prices to get the best deals, or to get to appointments on time. But the number system is composed of abstract symbols. To advance in math skills, young children need to learn what they mean . How would any of us know that the abstract numeral “5” represents the quantity of exactly five objects unless we had been taught? Foundational numeracy skills like counting, recognizing numbers and understanding quantity are related to future success in school, university and careers. The Assessment and Instruction for Mathematics (AIM) Collective is a network of researchers and educators committed to promoting the development of foundational numeracy skills across Canada . Researchers are familiar with evidence-based ways to assess children’s thinking and identify what skills are important for later success , and classroom educators are the experts at designing instructional activities to put this research into action . Here, as members of AIM, we explore some key foundational numeracy skills and offer practical examples of how adults can foster them to support children’s numeracy development. Counting and quantities During a child’s early years, they should have opportunities to practise counting, beginning with smaller ranges (for example, up to five or 10) and gradually progressing higher. Counting songs, like “Five Little Ducks,” and books like The Very Hungry Caterpillar are great ways to practise the count sequence. ‘Five Little Ducks’ sing-along from Ms. Rachel Toddler Learning Video. Practising the count sequence is important, but not sufficient, to support children’s developing numeracy. Young children can often recite the count sequence to five, 10 or even 20 before they really understand what the number words refer to. If you ask a three-year-old who can recite numbers up to five to give you five goldfish crackers from a bowl, a child who has not yet linked the words to the quantities they represent may grab a handful of crackers. They have not yet learned how to use counting to find out how many objects are in a set, or to create a set of an exact number. To help children learn to link the numbers to the quantities they represent, children should also have opportunities to practise counting objects, and matching different representations of number . For example, playing a game like “Tiny Polka Dots” requires matching cards with numerals: like a “3” matched with images of three polka dots arranged in varied ways. Patterning and ordering Being able to use numbers with ease requires knowing not just the quantities numbers represent, but also the relations between the number symbols themselves. Once children have mastered the count sequence, they should then move on to practise skip counting (for example, by twos or fives). Researchers found that kindergarteners were much quicker at recognizing that the numerals 1, 2, 3 were in order than they were at recognizing that 2, 4, 6 were in order. Many children said 2, 4, 6 were not in order because they aren’t next to each other in the count sequence. Activities putting different sequences in order along a number line can help children better understand relations between numbers. Order applies to more than just numbers, and children can also practise putting things in order from smallest to biggest, or putting sequences of events in order. Calendar routines in early years classrooms are another great way to show children how to use numbers to represent the passing of time, and to show sequences larger than 10. Place value In the base-10 number system, a numeral’s position determines its value. For example, in the number 356, the numeral “3” represents 300 (three hundreds), the numeral “5” represents 50 (five tens), and the numeral “6” represents six (six ones). As a precursor to formally investigating place value, younger children can be encouraged to bundle items into groups of 10 during playtime. (Chrissy Johnson1/Flickr) , CC BY Understanding this positional principle is essential for building children’s understanding of multi-digit numbers . Although children may intuitively recognize that larger numbers are generally longer than shorter ones , a solid understanding of place value enables them to develop a deeper and more accurate understanding of how multi-digit numbers are structured and represented. To reinforce the notion of place value, children can be encouraged to represent multi-digit numbers with concrete materials, like base-10 blocks and objects bundled into groups of 10 (for example: popsicle sticks, straws), as well as visual tools, such as place value charts and as 10 frames. Activities that focus on combining and breaking apart numbers by place value, like number bonds, can also strengthen children’s knowledge of multi-digit numbers. Importantly, mathematics learning is hierarchical, and more advanced skills build on foundational ones . By supporting young children’s emerging understanding of number, we can help them develop strong foundations to support their later mathematics learning. Rebecca Merkley receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada and Mitacs. Alexandra (Sandy) Youmans receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.

articles.content: Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession. Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 per cent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite. These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time. We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle. The challenge of metabolic adaptation Research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life , blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol , strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work. We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex. Obesity medication is an important pillar of obesity management and should be monitored as part of a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach to care. (Obesity Canada) , CC BY-NC-ND Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food. When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis . Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau. Emerging areas of research Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories. Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term. We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization . We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive. The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration. Personalized approaches to obesity At the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter . This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use . This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise. We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches. Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment. This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey. Lifestyle changes for success Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes. Current guidelines recommend people using GLP-1 medications to engage in resistance exercise to optimize their body composition for the best results. (Obesity Canada) , CC BY-NC-ND These include improving your nutrition by increasing protein intake and prioritizing fresh foods , such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins like fish and poultry , nuts and seeds. It’s important to eat small portions at consistent times throughout the day, avoid skipping meals, pay attention to your hunger and fullness cues and choose water as your beverage of choice. It’s also recommended to engage in resistance exercise to support muscle and bone health and achieve the best results. These strategies may help limit reductions in energy use as the weight comes off. Giovanna Guimaraes Lopes Bergamasco receives funding from the Alberta Diabetes Institute and the Alberta Diabetes Foundation. Andrea M. Haqq is a study principal investigator for clinical trials with Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, Eli Lilly, and Novo Nordisk. Dr. Prado reports speaking engagements and/or consultancy for Abbott Nutrition, Nestle Health Science, Nutricia, and Novo Nordisk. Rachel J. Skow does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Bell Canada’s AI Fabric data centre near Regina, Sask., has been touted as the “single largest private-sector capital investment” in Canadian history . Bell Canada says the project will use energy responsibly “without competing for local power resources.” But local residents have expressed concerns about the project’s potential water and electricity use. The data centre will require up to 1.2 gigawatts of electricity once fully operational, with 300 megawatts (MW) coming from the provincial power grid and 900 MWs from a dedicated, onsite bring-your-own-power scheme. The provincial Crown electric utility, SaskPower , currently has a mixed power generation portfolio of hydro, wind, solar, coal and natural gas. Most of its capacity comes from fossil fuels despite Saskatchewan having some of the country’s strongest wind and solar resources . Bell Canada says the facility will use a sealed, closed-loop water-cooling system paired with an air-cooled heat-rejection system. This system would not be connected to groundwater or the municipal water supply. However, that only accounts for the water used to operate the data centre itself. It does not include the water used by the electricity grid that provides power for the data centre. My dissertation research is focused on integrated water resource management in the Prairie Pothole region with a geographic focus on the Assiniboine River basin where this new data centre is located. Cooling data centres and power plants Dry cooling systems can expel heat; however, they require large fans and radiators to move heat into the environment and generally use more power. Wet cooling systems take advantage of water’s high latent heat of vaporization, much like our bodies do with sweating, to expel heat into the environment. Therefore, a reliable water source is required to continuously move water and the waste heat into the environment, much like how we need to drink water after sweating. Most electricity generation today remains highly water-intensive. According to SaskPower’s 2025-26 annual report , around 25 per cent of Saskatchewan’s power generation capacity comes from coal-fired plants. If the grid allocates 300 MW of power to Bell Canada’s data centre, cooling water will still need to be used elsewhere, far from the data centre. Saskatchewan’s current coal-powered plants use a combination of dry and wet cooling technologies. If built, small modular reactors located along the Rafferty Reservoir would require similar cooling techniques to operate. Read more: Are small nuclear reactors the solution to Canada’s net-zero ambitions? The provincial government has announced plans to refurbish and extend the life of three coal-fired power plants in southern Saskatchewan: Poplar River, Shand and Boundary Dam. Coal is planned as a bridge power source until planned nuclear reactors come online. Data centres might employ closed-loop cooling systems that reduce onsite water demand. However, that’s only one half of the water-accounting equation. To get a complete picture of their water use, data centres must factor in both onsite water use and the water used elsewhere to generate the power they need. Given the distance between Saskatchewan’s southern coal plants and the data centre near Regina, water demand will likely shift from one place to another . The total water withdrawn from the ecosystem may increase far from where the data centre is located. Using natural gas to power data centres If Saskatchewan follows Alberta’s path and uses natural gas to power data centres, it will take water to drill for, extract, process and deliver natural gas to customers. Saskatchewan has relatively little natural gas production . That means much of the natural gas will likely be imported from Alberta gas fields. The province can experience large seasonal swings in precipitation and temperatures. The amount of water entering supply reservoirs in the Assiniboine River basin can change on an annual basis. Yet, demand for water from industry, power generation, agriculture and municipalities isn’t always able to adapt to seasonal changes in river flows. Carefully managing water supplies will be an ongoing challenge in the region to settle this water balance discrepancy. More research will be needed to better understand changing flow-generating mechanisms in the region. In the Prairies, these mechanisms can include how water enters soils during the spring snowmelt or how wetlands fill up and subsequently spill into neighbouring streams. Authorities will need to consider the cumulative effects of increased water demand in the area, especially during prolonged droughts , to ensure they conserve finite water resources. Corwyn Shomachuk has received funding through NSERC Water Health CREATE, the NRCan Flood Hazard Identification and Mapping Program and the Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure Research Grant. He is Board Director of the Canadian Water Resources Association, Saskatchewan Branch President of the Global Institute of Water Security Students and Young Researchers Association and a constituency association executive member of the Saskatchewan NDP.

Coal is planned as a bridge power source until planned nuclear reactors come online. Data centres might employ closed-loop cooling systems that reduce onsite water demand. However, that’s only one half of the water-accounting equation. To get a complete picture of their water use, data centres must factor in both onsite water use and the water used elsewhere to generate the power they need. Given the distance between Saskatchewan’s southern coal plants and the data centre near Regina, water demand will likely shift from one place to another . The total water withdrawn from the ecosystem may increase far from where the data centre is located. Using natural gas to power data centres If Saskatchewan follows Alberta’s path and uses natural gas to power data centres, it will take water to drill for, extract, process and deliver natural gas to customers. Saskatchewan has relatively little natural gas production . That means much of the natural gas will likely be imported from Alberta gas fields. The province can experience large seasonal swings in precipitation and temperatures. The amount of water entering supply reservoirs in the Assiniboine River basin can change on an annual basis. Yet, demand for water from industry, power generation, agriculture and municipalities isn’t always able to adapt to seasonal changes in river flows. Carefully managing water supplies will be an ongoing challenge in the region to settle this water balance discrepancy. More research will be needed to better understand changing flow-generating mechanisms in the region. In the Prairies, these mechanisms can include how water enters soils during the spring snowmelt or how wetlands fill up and subsequently spill into neighbouring streams. Authorities will need to consider the cumulative effects of increased water demand in the area, especially during prolonged droughts , to ensure they conserve finite water resources. Corwyn Shomachuk has received funding through NSERC Water Health CREATE, the NRCan Flood Hazard Identification and Mapping Program and the Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure Research Grant. He is Board Director of the Canadian Water Resources Association, Saskatchewan Branch President of the Global Institute of Water Security Students and Young Researchers Association and a constituency association executive member of the Saskatchewan NDP.
articles.title: Data centres may consume far more water than developers suggest

articles.content: Much of the news coverage on young men recently has focused on social media, gambling and the online “manosphere.” But some of the most consequential changes in young men’s lives are happening in school and workplaces. Men, on average, continue to have advantages in the labour market. But some groups of men face significant disadvantages, and factors such as social class, race and migrant background can make an enormous difference to their educational and employment prospects. This distinction is often lost in debates about the supposed crisis facing young men. Debates are often framed as a culture war that pits men’s concerns against women’s progress. Some point to the persistent gender pay gap and the continued over-representation of men in the most senior jobs. Others point to young men who drop out of school and end up unemployed. International Men’s Day — Nov. 19 — provides an opportunity to move beyond claims about whether men are “falling behind” and instead ask which men are struggling, and why. Men missing from equity conversations Men who experience disadvantage receive surprisingly little attention in research on workplace inequality. In our recent paper , we reviewed research from several western countries — mainly the United States, United Kingdom and parts of the European Union — on the career barriers facing men from disadvantaged backgrounds. We searched Google Scholar for intersectional studies of gender and found 1,330 studies with “women” in the title, compared with 234 mentioning “men.” The difference was even larger in research on career advancement. Studies examining the promotion of women into workplace roles, while also considering race or ethnicity, outnumbered comparable studies of men by about 80 to one. There are good reasons why equity research has focused so strongly on women. Women have historically faced — and continue to face — substantial barriers in education and employment. But this focus has left us knowing much less about men who do not share the advantages typically associated with being male. Treating men as a single group can obscure the experiences of those who are struggling. The gap often starts in school Inequalities often begin well before people enter the workplace. Boys from low-income families and racialized or stigmatized migrant backgrounds tend to fall behind at school. One factor may be teacher expectations . Research suggests students are more likely to finish school when their teachers expect more of them. If disadvantaged boys are perceived as less likely to succeed, those expectations can become a self-fulfilling cycle. According to social scientist Richard Reeves , young men in the United States are almost 50 per cent more likely than young women to drop out of high school. Canada shows a very similar gap, although the pattern varies by background and level of education. The 2021 census shows that about one-quarter of Canadian-born men aged 25 to 34 held a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared with almost 40 per cent of Canadian-born women in the same age group. These educational disadvantages increasingly shape what happens later in the labour market . A changing labour market The labour market that once provided relatively well-paid opportunities for less-educated men has changed over the years. A generation ago, a young man could leave school early and still find reasonably well-paid manual work. In 1970, high school dropouts held 43 per cent of American manufacturing jobs . By 2016, fewer than 10 per cent of those jobs were held by workers who had not finished high school. Many of those jobs have disappeared, and those that remain increasingly require formal qualifications. At the same time, employers place greater value on cognitive , interpersonal and communication skills . Research on class and gender stereotypes shows that cognitive and interpersonal skills are more strongly associated with upper-class men, while working-class men are more likely to be associated with physical strength and toughness. Meanwhile, employment is growing in health care, education, administration and literacy occupations. An aging population is increasing the demand for care workers. Advances in artificial intelligence are likely to make interpersonal and emotional skills more important because they are difficult for machines to replicate. However, men remain substantially under-represented in much of this work. In Canada, about 91 per cent of regulated nurses are women, and only about 25 per cent of elementary and high school teachers are men. Many working-class men have neither been prepared for these occupations nor encouraged to see them as realistic career choices. Some avoid them because caring and service work conflicts with their idea of what a man’s job is . The result is a mismatch between where jobs are growing and where men have been encouraged to look for work. Seeing men working as teachers, nurses and care workers can help boys imagine these careers for themselves rather than assuming they are meant for women. (Unsplash) Equity is not a zero-sum game Attention to men’s disadvantage is often met with resistance . We encountered this when we presented an early version of our paper at conferences. One concern was that supporting disadvantaged men could come at the expense of women’s gains by diverting attention or resources from them. But improving opportunities for disadvantaged men does not require reversing progress for women. French economists, for example, have argued that revaluing female-dominated occupations would advance pay equity for women while also draw more men into this work . Raising wages in undervalued care work would help the women already doing it while opening a door for men. There is evidence this can happen. A French study found that male midwives helped the profession’s push for better recognition . Bringing more men into areas such as health care could also address staff shortages in sectors that remain overwhelmingly made up of women . Equity for women and opportunities for disadvantaged men can both be pursued through the same policies, in many cases. What can we do There are broader consequences to leaving disadvantaged men behind. People who believe that economic and social institutions have failed them can become receptive to political messages built around resentment and grievance . But this is not simply about preventing political radicalization. Stable work, economic security and a sense of purpose are important to individual and social well-being. Schools can pay closer attention to expectations for boys who are at risk of disengaging. Governments and employers can strengthen vocational pathways into occupations with labour shortages, rather than training young people for jobs that are disappearing. Children also need to see more men working as teachers, nurses and care workers. Seeing men in these roles can help boys imagine these careers for themselves rather than assuming they are meant for women. International Men’s Day should be an occasion to have a more nuanced conversation about the men being left behind. Men, on average, remain advantaged in many areas of social and economic life. But not all men share those advantages, and understanding why is an important part of understanding inequality itself. Eddy Ng receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada. articles.content: Each summer, Pride fills the streets across Canada. Pride Toronto organizers estimated 3.1 million attendees in 2024 , and more than 900,000 people took part in Fierté Montréal in 2025 . Smaller cities turn out too: about 7,600 attended Windsor-Essex Pride Fest in 2025 . Canada has some of the world’s strongest legal protections for 2SLGBTQI+ people, scoring 94 out of 100 on Equaldex’s legal index as of November 2026. It also presents itself as a refuge. Ottawa resettles up to 250 2SLGBTQI+ refugees a year referred by Rainbow Railroad, and claims based on sexual orientation or gender identity have made up about six per cent of all refugee claims in recent years. Read more: BIPOC or IBPOC? LGBTQ or LGBTQ2S+? Who decides which terms we should use? But for Black queer and trans newcomers who fled persecution, a harder question remains once the parade ends. Legal protection is not the same as belonging. And the thing that most reliably builds belonging — community — is among the least reliably funded. Isolated from every direction As a scholar whose research examines the intersections of migration and LGBTQ+ sexualities, I conducted focus groups with 22 members of the Queer and Trans Migrant Advocacy Alliance of Windsor-Essex (QTMAAWE) in the summer of 2025. The peer-led organization was founded in 2024 by and for queer and trans migrants. All participants identified as Black, and most were refugee claimants from Nigeria, Tanzania, Kenya and Zambia. The findings appear in a community research report released in August. Windsor, Ont., is a telling place to ask these questions. As a mid-sized border city, it receives a significant share of Canada’s asylum seekers . Yet until QTMAAWE, no organization in the region catered specifically to Black queer and trans migrants. Participants described profound isolation, often from the moment they arrived. Many, like Ivan (participants’ names are pseudonyms), had been cut off by family. He said: “I message them, I text them, I call them. No response.” In addition, spaces meant to feel safe often were not. Many felt shut out of their own ethnic and faith communities. Susan recalled visiting a local queer-affirming church: “It was just white people […] I’ve never felt Black in my life — I felt so Black.” The consequences of this isolation can be severe. As Daniel told me: “After a year, I ended up getting hospitalized because of loneliness. It affected me mentally in a very serious way.” Community as the intervention In that context, participants described QTMAAWE in words rarely used for a service agency. Asked what it represents, one group answered: freedom, home, family, peace. The organization now connects roughly 600 members. It runs weekly safe-space gatherings and helps people prepare refugee claims, find jobs and navigate housing and health care. One participant said more than 50 people were hired at a single QTMAAWE job fair. Community participation even carries legal weight. Support letters and attendance records help claimants document their identities for refugee hearings, which matters for people who survived at home by leaving no trace. Just as important are the shared meals. Ivan described a potluck where someone brought one of his favourite dishes from home. “We used our hands to eat it, and we all had fun,” he said. “And I felt like, this is where I belong.” This is not only a Windsor story, however. In a national survey of more than 400 Black 2SLGBTQI+ people for The Enchanté Network’s Back to Our Roots report , 85 per cent said they had experienced anti-Black racism in 2SLGBTQI+ spaces. Organizers called for a national Black 2SLGBTQI+ organization “by us and for us.” Federal data point the same way. In the federal government’s 2019-20 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan Survey , Black African respondents were less likely than the overall sample to feel included in queer community spaces (50 per cent versus 62 per cent) or to feel a strong sense of belonging to Canada (66 per cent versus 82 per cent). All of this suggests that Black-led, migrant-led peer organizations may offer one of the most effective ways to ease isolation for these newcomers. Belonging on borrowed time Yet this work remains precariously funded. QTMAAWE has received no money from the Federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan , the $100-million program Ottawa launched in 2022. In October, the organization joined more than 40 groups on Parliament Hill calling for the plan’s renewal. Budget 2026 delivered part of what they asked for: $60 million over four years starting in 2027-28, plus $15 million in ongoing annual funding. Public debate in Canada rarely treats belonging as something worth funding. Coverage tends to frame 2SLGBTQI+ newcomers through persecution abroad or, more recently, through Bill C-12’s one-year rule , under which claims made more than a year after arrival are no longer referred to the Immigration and Refugee Board. Policy proposals call for culturally informed mental health services . These are real needs, but such proposals overlook the peer-led spaces where racism, homophobia, transphobia and immigration precarity are confronted together. In Windsor, the result is an essential institution that relies on borrowed space and rests on very few shoulders, above all those of its founder, Anold Mulaisho. He said: “If you’re not going to give me a seat at the table. I’m going to create my own table.” Funding belonging year-round So what would it take to fund belonging year-round in mid-sized cities like Windsor? Participants were clear. First, a permanent, accessible community space, which participants named as their single most important need. Second, core operating funding rather than short-term project grants. Third, reliable referral pathways from shelters, settlement agencies, clinics and legal aid, so newcomers don’t have to rely on luck to find community. Fourth, recognition that shared meals, peer support and safe-space gatherings are mental health infrastructure, not extras. Pride began as advocacy, not only celebration. For Black queer and trans newcomers, honouring that history means making sure Canada’s welcome lasts longer than one festival each summer. Carlo Handy Charles has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) and the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation. Carlo Handy Charles is also a Visiting Scholar in the Department of Sociology at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor and a Fellow at the CNRS French Collaborative Institute on Migration (Institut Convergences Migrations) in Paris.

articles.content: Peekachu, Rain, Osiris, Caspian, Jellybean and Cyprus are dead . They were six of the 30 beluga whales removed from Marineland in Niagara Falls earlier this year. Echo is dead too. She was one of the four dolphins who were also removed around the same time. For all intents and purposes, she was blind . I think about the rocks and paint that have been found in the belugas’ stomachs through autopsies. I dwell on how a place designed to hold them captive was legitimized for years. Jellybean was born at Marineland 19 years ago and gave birth there, too. My profession — planning — had a role to play in facilitating their deaths and in allowing suffering during their lives. Planning has many specializations: urban, rural, regional, housing and transportation are a few. I am a Registered Professional Planner who specialized in environmental planning during graduate school. My work over the past 20 years, though, has often been more about what land can be used for and how it’s used. Marineland has been around since the 1960s. Its record of bad things happening to animals only grew over time . I can now see how the mistreatment of the whales and dolphins was inevitable. The orientation of planning Planning has been a formal occupation in Canada since 1919 . It has the legal status of a self-regulating profession now. Planners often work for governments, especially municipalities. Personally, I’ve analyzed land-use plans as a consultant. In my work for a provincial government, I’ve told other planners what needs to change before a plan or its implementing bylaw can be approved. And as a municipal planner, I’ve made decisions about how humans can use land. The City of Niagara Falls’ Official Plan describes Marineland as “family entertainment.” No words in this legal planning document speak to the conditions the sea mammals needed to survive, let alone thrive. Yet it’s the document that legitimized Marineland’s existence. The nails in the coffins A February 2025 Committee of Adjustment meeting haunts me. Committees of Adjustment are a sub-structure of municipal governments in Ontario. They are allowed under Section 44 of the provincial government’s Planning Act . Committees of Adjustment make decisions about proposed changes to land that are minor, and that also don’t meet the requirements in municipal planning documents. Since these committees are a planning mechanism, planning staff help them do their work. The Niagara Falls committee considered eight different applications about Marineland in February 2025. Each was approved . Together, they brought Marineland into compliance with the city’s Official Plan and Zoning Bylaw. Niagara Falls adopted a new Official Plan in August 2026, which is still awaiting approval from the provincial government. Many wheels need to be set in motion before an actual application to eventually redevelop land materializes. This was one of those wheels. After the February 2025 meeting, Marineland applied for federal approval to export the whales and dolphins (which was at first denied), then said that it would euthanize them (more than once) and finally received federal approval to export them. Hierarchies of power and public processes The planning process can be the only public opportunity to point out something that could, otherwise, go unnoticed. At the February 2025 meeting, people expressed concerns about what would happen to Marineland’s whales and dolphins. Some attendees asked the committee to defer its decision until there was more information about how the animals on the site would be treated. Marineland’s representative suggested that the approvals they sought were unrelated to animal welfare . Marineland had asked for variances, easements, new parcel creation and mortgage release to secure operational financing. The municipality’s planners had evaluated the applications as minor, based on how there was no actual development being proposed, how no neighbouring properties would be impacted and how streetscape and character wouldn’t be compromised. If it sounds like jargon, that’s because it is. Over time, planning has become a profession with its own language and processes. Often, when I’m talking to a non-planner, I’m simply translating. The planning priorities in the jargon are not unusual either. Mechanisms like Committees of Adjustment have also been called out for reducing greater public participation . Finding a better way Peekachu, Rain, Osiris, Caspian, Jellybean, Cyprus and Echo didn’t fit into the planning process. Sweden-based planning theorist Jonathan Metzger calls the effect “radical exclusion.” As a practitioner who has turned to a PhD, I’m painfully aware that planners think not in terms of life, but land. The Canadian planning profession’s most recent update to its ethical standards doesn’t do animals justice either. Marineland’s tanks and enclosures may be empty now. Fur farms, factory farms, testing labs and zoos still stand. The path to different futures is not easy. Animals are legally property. So is land. There is urgency, though, and a need for answers that are kinder than the status quo. In their new book , Animals and The Right to Politics , philosophy scholars Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka imagine a city with two distinct governance systems. In addition to the existing municipal government, they propose a new political entity that takes over land and development decisions. The intention is to create a more stable, peaceful world for animals. Plausible or not, we must move towards some new normal. Humanity is a hollow word if we don’t. But I don’t see it happening unless non-planners insist that planning work consider every sentient being, not just humans. Pooja Kumar received the Ontario Graduate Scholarship (2026-2027) to generally support her PhD studies. She is a Member of the Canadian Institute of Planners and the Prince Edward Island Institute of Professional Planners. She became a Registered Professional Planner in 2010, with the Ontario Professional Planners Institute.

I am a Registered Professional Planner who specialized in environmental planning during graduate school. My work over the past 20 years, though, has often been more about what land can be used for and how it’s used. Marineland has been around since the 1960s. Its record of bad things happening to animals only grew over time . I can now see how the mistreatment of the whales and dolphins was inevitable. The orientation of planning Planning has been a formal occupation in Canada since 1919 . It has the legal status of a self-regulating profession now. Planners often work for governments, especially municipalities. Personally, I’ve analyzed land-use plans as a consultant. In my work for a provincial government, I’ve told other planners what needs to change before a plan or its implementing bylaw can be approved. And as a municipal planner, I’ve made decisions about how humans can use land. The City of Niagara Falls’ Official Plan describes Marineland as “family entertainment.” No words in this legal planning document speak to the conditions the sea mammals needed to survive, let alone thrive. Yet it’s the document that legitimized Marineland’s existence. The nails in the coffins A February 2025 Committee of Adjustment meeting haunts me. Committees of Adjustment are a sub-structure of municipal governments in Ontario. They are allowed under Section 44 of the provincial government’s Planning Act . Committees of Adjustment make decisions about proposed changes to land that are minor, and that also don’t meet the requirements in municipal planning documents. Since these committees are a planning mechanism, planning staff help them do their work. The Niagara Falls committee considered eight different applications about Marineland in February 2025. Each was approved . Together, they brought Marineland into compliance with the city’s Official Plan and Zoning Bylaw. Niagara Falls adopted a new Official Plan in August 2026, which is still awaiting approval from the provincial government. Many wheels need to be set in motion before an actual application to eventually redevelop land materializes. This was one of those wheels. After the February 2025 meeting, Marineland applied for federal approval to export the whales and dolphins (which was at first denied), then said that it would euthanize them (more than once) and finally received federal approval to export them. Hierarchies of power and public processes The planning process can be the only public opportunity to point out something that could, otherwise, go unnoticed. At the February 2025 meeting, people expressed concerns about what would happen to Marineland’s whales and dolphins. Some attendees asked the committee to defer its decision until there was more information about how the animals on the site would be treated. Marineland’s representative suggested that the approvals they sought were unrelated to animal welfare . Marineland had asked for variances, easements, new parcel creation and mortgage release to secure operational financing. The municipality’s planners had evaluated the applications as minor, based on how there was no actual development being proposed, how no neighbouring properties would be impacted and how streetscape and character wouldn’t be compromised. If it sounds like jargon, that’s because it is. Over time, planning has become a profession with its own language and processes. Often, when I’m talking to a non-planner, I’m simply translating. The planning priorities in the jargon are not unusual either. Mechanisms like Committees of Adjustment have also been called out for reducing greater public participation . Finding a better way Peekachu, Rain, Osiris, Caspian, Jellybean, Cyprus and Echo didn’t fit into the planning process. Sweden-based planning theorist Jonathan Metzger calls the effect “radical exclusion.” As a practitioner who has turned to a PhD, I’m painfully aware that planners think not in terms of life, but land. The Canadian planning profession’s most recent update to its ethical standards doesn’t do animals justice either. Marineland’s tanks and enclosures may be empty now. Fur farms, factory farms, testing labs and zoos still stand. The path to different futures is not easy. Animals are legally property. So is land. There is urgency, though, and a need for answers that are kinder than the status quo. In their new book , Animals and The Right to Politics , philosophy scholars Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka imagine a city with two distinct governance systems. In addition to the existing municipal government, they propose a new political entity that takes over land and development decisions. The intention is to create a more stable, peaceful world for animals. Plausible or not, we must move towards some new normal. Humanity is a hollow word if we don’t. But I don’t see it happening unless non-planners insist that planning work consider every sentient being, not just humans. Pooja Kumar received the Ontario Graduate Scholarship (2026-2027) to generally support her PhD studies. She is a Member of the Canadian Institute of Planners and the Prince Edward Island Institute of Professional Planners. She became a Registered Professional Planner in 2010, with the Ontario Professional Planners Institute.
articles.title: Was a kinder fate possible for Marineland’s animals? How the planning process failed them

articles.content: Sighting a humpback whale from a boat can be awe-inspiring. For some BC Ferries passengers, that experience became disturbing when their ferry struck and fatally injured a humpback whale on Oct. 18. The whale was later identified as BCX1700 , nicknamed Notcho. Notcho’s death, and the ceremony Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) held to honour him, made national news . Coverage of Notcho’s death may elicit feelings of anger, sadness or despair. These are forms of what is called ecological grief : the emotional response caused by experiencing or learning about environmental destruction, species extinction, biodiversity loss and climate change. Effective ways to cope with ecological grief depend on the situation and the person . A common suggestion for people feeling ecological grief is to take action. In Notcho’s case, the Marine Education and Research Society provided practical solutions for preventing future ship strikes based on the details of his death. Online responses from members of the public to the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw ceremony show that mourning practices can also be helpful for coping. Notcho’s story North Pacific humpback whales are a conservation success story in many ways. Their populations have been recovering since they were legally protected from commercial whaling in 1966. Unfortunately, as their numbers in the Salish Sea increase, so does the risk of ship strikes . The same behaviour that allows people to enjoy them — spending time at the surface feeding or resting — also puts them at risk of collisions with boats. Fatal ship strikes of whales are not unusual, and there are specific reasons Notcho’s death became a national news story: his fatal injury was preventable, traumatic and witnessed up close by several people. He had a name and had been known in the area for almost 10 years. Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw recognized Notcho as a relative and honoured him accordingly . Ecological grief is normal and healthy Ecological grief can be experienced in relation to many types of ecological losses , such as individual animals like Notcho, cherished trees like the Golden Spruce or entire species and ecosystems, to name just a few. It can also be felt in response to the impacts of climate change . Researchers, and the public more broadly, increasingly understand ecological grief as a healthy and valid emotional response . As with any form of grief, mourning is a beneficial, and even necessary, process for coping with emotions. Ecological grief itself has been well-studied and described, but effective ways of coping with it, and of mourning ecological losses, are not as well understood . Coping with ecological losses I have spent my career working in conservation biology, and this is not my first brush with ecological grief. It’s an unfortunate occupational hazard . I recently returned to academia to investigate strategies for coping with it. Through my preliminary research, I have been exploring three forms of coping : action-focused (or problem-solving), emotion-focused and meaning-focused. When I heard the news about Notcho and went online for more information, I noticed evidence of all three in public reactions to a post made by Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw on their Facebook page about an honouring ceremony for Notcho. On Facebook, members of the public expressed action-focused reactions when they conveyed frustration about ferry speed limits in the area and called for changes. Some people wanted to know if his body would be returned to the ocean to provide nourishment to the marine ecosystem as a form of ecological restoration action. People also used words and emojis to express sorrow, heartbreak and love, which can be a form of emotion-focused coping. Meaning-focused coping may take the form of developing mourning practices. For Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw, mourning Notcho meant bringing him to their territory so “(we) could care for his remains in accordance with our laws,” and honouring him with a sacred ceremony . Many online responses expressed gratitude for the ceremony. Making meaning through mourning The need for specific mourning practices, like ceremonies or rituals, to mourn ecological losses was identified more than 30 years ago by Phyllis Windle, an ecologist and hospital chaplain. When it comes to ecological grief, some people may lack spiritual traditions to support them. Meaningful rituals can be difficult to create in a secularized society, and without precedent or cultural guidance, people may not know how to make meaning from these losses. Facebook users responding to the honouring ceremony of Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw demonstrated their desire for meaning-making through mourning practices in a variety of ways, from thanking everyone caring for Notcho’s journey, to expressing gratitude for learning about the honouring ceremony, to creating their own mourning practices. While some people find Indigenous beliefs and ceremonial practices inspiring , non-Indigenous people need to create practices rooted in their own beliefs and values . As a non-Indigenous person from Ontario, I do not claim any connection to Notcho or the waters he lived in, apart from a brief, magical encounter with a pod of breaching humpbacks in northern British Columbia a decade ago. Nonetheless, I cried when I heard how Notcho died and as I read people’s responses. I wondered whether the ferry passengers who witnessed his fatal injury experienced a form of secondary trauma and how they will cope. I also think about the conservation organizations and volunteers who love these whales and give their time to advocate for them. Do they have the practices and supports they need to mourn when they lose a whale they know? As an outsider, it may not be my place to create my own ritual for Notcho. What I have found is that telling a part of his story, with gratitude to those who knew him, has become my small way of making meaning from his death. Perhaps that is where many of us can begin when we experience ecological grief: we can let ourselves feel both love and sorrow for whales and other non-human parts of nature. And we can respectfully create ways of marking these losses that reflect our own values. Ecological grief is a sign of how much we care . Corina Brdar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
