articles.title: Mourning Notcho: What one whale’s death teaches us about ecological grief

articles.content: Delegates from around the world are currently gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31 . Among the issues up for discussion will be an important question: who should pay for the harms caused by climate change? One study estimated that between 1850 and 2015, the Global North was responsible for 92 per cent of the carbon dioxide emissions that exceeded countries’ fair shares of a safe global limit. The United Nations Fund for responding to Loss and Damage , established at the 2022 COP in Egypt, has received requests from 119 countries seeking US$2.8 billion in funding , far more than the US$342 million allocated to its start-up phase. Canada committed CA$16 million , while the United States, the largest historical emitter, pledged US$17.5 million, then withdrew from the fund’s board in 2025. Decisions on the first regular round of funding requests are expected in December 2026 , but Nigeria’s environment minister expressed the frustration of many when he said in June that the fund “ looks like a mirage .” Behind the struggle over loss and damage is a question that extends beyond climate finance. What responsibilities do institutions that benefited from carbon-intensive development bear toward those living with the consequences, especially when some losses cannot be undone? Universities have their own climate debt to confront. “Climate change and planetary destruction have been accelerated, in large part, by technologies developed in universities,” as one of us, Mateus Tremembé, has written . Universities and climate change Universities have helped build and sustain the carbon-intensive economy in several ways. They have produced much of the knowledge it runs on, from petroleum engineering to economic models that treat continuous growth as a measure of progress . They have trained professionals who design, manage and finance that economy, often reinforcing the idea that land and nature are resources to be extracted. And many have maintained financial ties with fossil-fuel companies through research partnerships, donations and investments. Research can also reproduce extractive relationships, even in projects meant to help communities adapt to climate change. Local and Indigenous communities often contribute significant knowledge, labour and data , while academic researchers frequently retain control over the questions, funding, data and interpretation, and recognition flows disproportionately to universities. This imbalance runs counter to the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance and article 31 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples , which affirm Indigenous Peoples’ authority over their knowledge and data. Addressing these patterns requires a reparative approach to climate research: one built on long-term accountability to communities and their lands, redistributing resources and authority, and treating Indigenous and local knowledge as expertise rather than raw material. Research cannot undo irreversible losses. But where communities invite collaboration, it can support their efforts to respond to ecological change on their own terms. Importance of shared authority The distinction between providing resources and sharing authority is also central to debates over climate finance. The loss and damage fund describes its approach as “bottom-up, country-led and country-owned” , with provisions for local engagement. This is meant to counter the longstanding tendency for climate finance priorities to be set by international institutions and donors. But country ownership is not the same as community control . In many countries, governments have long made decisions about Indigenous lands and lives without Indigenous consent. Requiring national government endorsement does not guarantee that Indigenous Peoples will decide how losses in their territories are defined or addressed. This matters especially because many climate losses cannot be fully measured in money . They may involve broken relationships with rivers, plants and animals, cultural practices tied to place, or knowledge passed between generations. When governments and funders define losses only in monetary terms, these dimensions can disappear from view , along with communities’ own priorities for responding to them. Community-directed research Adaptation seeks to reduce climate risks. Loss and damage concerns harms that cannot be fully prevented or reversed. Both raise questions about who defines harm, what should be sustained or repaired and who directs the response. These questions inform our work on community-directed adaptation research , or C-DAR. The premise is simple but demanding: communities should lead in setting research questions and making decisions, with as much control over resources as possible. In Ceará, northeastern Brazil, the Tremembé da Barra do Mundaú Indigenous people are facing environmental pressures that affect their way of life, with climate change expected to bring more severe droughts and extreme rainfall . The community is developing collaborative research initiatives to strengthen traditional food systems , including collective farming, environmental education for young people and phasing out the use of pesticides. The Tremembé people have also drawn up their Territorial and Environmental Management Plan , a document that sets out community priorities for the management of natural resources and for maintaining traditional knowledge and practices. More than just a planning document, it represents a collective commitment to present and future generations: that children born in the territory will have access to drinking water, clean rivers, healthy fish, living forests and ancestral knowledge that is practised and passed on. For the Tremembé, protecting biodiversity also means ensuring the continuity of life, culture and relationships with their land. Repair involves sustaining the knowledge, practices and territorial conditions that communities identify as necessary for their collective futures. Following communities’ lead Under a community-directed adaptation approach, communities decide what data are collected, how they are used and who controls them. Academic research partners can support these efforts by following the community’s lead and contributing their skills when invited. In Tremembé territories, academic partners have supported the installation of weather stations to record rainfall and temperature, and young people are involved in assessing water security. The aim is to bring these data into conversation with Elders’ knowledge of how springs and rivers have changed and to inform climate adaptation planning. Ultimately, the value of such research should not be measured only by whether it contributes to academic knowledge, but by whether it strengthens a community’s ability to monitor ecological change, make adaptation decisions and sustain knowledge and relationships across generations. Communities are already responding to climate change, drawing on generational knowledge and relationships with their territories. Universities can contribute expertise, resources and infrastructure, but doing so requires following communities’ priorities and rethinking established research practices. As climate finance begins to tackle loss and damage, universities should begin confronting their own climate debt by shifting control over research priorities and resources toward communities. Sharon Stein receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada. articles.content: In July 2022, the late Pope Francis came to Canada seeking forgiveness for the Catholic Church’s role in the residential school system, acknowledging it as genocide . His penitential pilgrimage was intended to mark a new chapter in the relationship between the Catholic Church and Indigenous Peoples, calling for a renewed commitment of “ walking together .” Four years later, students at a Catholic high school in Grande Prairie, Alberta, offered a glimpse of what this commitment might look like in practice. On Oct. 13 , Indigenous and non-Indigenous students staged a demonstration to protest residential school denialism publicly endorsed by one of their social studies teachers on her personal Facebook page . They did so by walking out together. Their peaceful disobedience was more than an act of protest. It was an expression of solidarity, a collective refusal to dismiss Indigenous experiences and a reminder that reconciliation is advanced not only through institutional apologies, but through the actions of those willing to stand together against injustice. Challenge from inside Catholic institutions We are married writing partners and PhD students whose respective areas of study involve Catholic theology and religion curriculum in Catholic schools. We approach this research from Anishinaabe (Noah) and settler (Erenna) perspectives. We have previously examined how colonial ideologies of institutional leadership within Catholic education can undermine commitments to reconciliation . However, the Grande Prairie walkout offers an opportunity to consider the other side of this relationship: Students exercising their own agency at the grassroots level to challenge injustice from within a Catholic institution. Students were responding to a Facebook post by a social studies teacher at their high school on Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day . The post shared a statement from Maxime Bernier, the leader of the People’s Party of Canada, which partly reads: “ Let’s tell the truth: no bodies were found in Kamloops. The residential-school ‘genocide’ claim is a hoax .” The teacher added “Hear, hear!” on her status update. Read more: We fact-checked residential school denialists and debunked their ‘mass grave hoax’ theory In an interview, the teacher told CBC News she is “not a residential school denialist, which many people have framed me as.” Reconciliation, resistance and solidarity For reconciliation to be meaningful, it must amount to more than institutional apologies and commemorations, especially when members of those institutions undermine the commitments made. In Red Skin, White Masks , Dene political scientist Glen Sean Coulthard argues that reconciliation focused on institutional forgiveness, without radically transforming colonial relationships, leaves Indigenous people vulnerable to ongoing harms. This is similarly the case when institutions fail to adequately prevent denialism. Read more: 5 ways teachers can respond to residential school denialism in the classroom Combating these institutional shortcomings often requires resistance. Coulthard says resistance is not an obstacle to reconciliation but an expression of Indigenous agency and self-determination. Seen this way, the Grande Prairie walkout was more than a protest against one teacher’s posts: It was students refusing to let reconciliation remain an institutional promise. Equally significant was the solidarity of the students who walked out together. Coulthard and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, a Michi Saagiig Nishnaabeg scholar, describe solidarity rooted in mutual responsibility and collective resistance, not sympathy alone, in their article Grounded Normativity / Place-Based Solidarity . Such solidarity asks more of institutions that apologize while their own members or representatives deny the truth. It’s worth noting that the student walkout happened at a school named for Pope John Paul II, who in a 1979 address to young people stated: “ Liberation, even in the social sense, begins with knowledge and courageous proclamation of the truth .” Teaching for justice In a recent Warrior Life podcast interview, Mi'kmaw lawyer and author Pam Palmater spoke with Indigenous studies professor and writer Niigaan Sinclair and historian Sean Carleton about their newly published book, Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism . Sinclair, a member of Peguis First Nation, notes that for over a century, Canadians have been miseducated and misinformed about the residential school system — yet younger generations are generally now being exposed to either courses or credentialed research on the topic of truth and reconciliation . This learning, we argue, instils a strong sense of historical and information literacy. All generations need opportunities to learn the same, and to identify and counter residential schools denialism. Read more: Confronting residential schools denialism is an ethical and shared Canadian responsibility A desire to counter denialism was exemplified by the young adults who stood up for the injustice and false narrative they observed by a member of their school community. One student stated at the walkout: “ My grandma was in residential schools, and I just don’t think this is OK. articles.description: In July 2022, the late Pope Francis came to Canada seeking forgiveness for the Catholic Church’s role in the residential school system, acknowledging it as genocide . His penitential pilgrimage was intended to mark a new chapter in the relationship between the Catholic Church and Indigenous Peoples, calling for a renewed commitment of “ walking together .” Four years later, students at a Catholic high school in Grande Prairie, Alberta, offered a glimpse of what this commitment might look like in practice. On Oct. 13 , Indigenous and non-Indigenous students staged a demonstration to protest residential school denialism publicly endorsed by one of their social studies teachers on her personal Facebook page . They did so by walking out together. Their peaceful disobedience was more than an act of protest. It was an expression of solidarity, a collective refusal to dismiss Indigenous experiences and a reminder that reconciliation is advanced not only through institutional apologies, but through the actions of those willing to stand together against injustice. Challenge from inside Catholic institutions We are married writing partners and PhD students whose respective areas of study involve Catholic theology and religion curriculum in Catholic schools. We approach this research from Anishinaabe (Noah) and settler (Erenna) perspectives. We have previously examined how colonial ideologies of institutional leadership within Catholic education can undermine commitments to reconciliation . However, the Grande Prairie walkout offers an opportunity to consider the other side of this relationship: Students exercising their own agency at the grassroots level to challenge injustice from within a Catholic institution. Students were responding to a Facebook post by a social studies teacher at their high school on Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day . The post shared a statement from Maxime Bernier, the leader of the People’s Party of Canada, which partly reads: “ Let’s tell the truth: no bodies were found in Kamloops. articles.content: Facing tariffs and a deteriorating trade relationship, Canada has been looking to reduce its dependence on the United States, which still accounts for over 70 per cent of Canadian goods exports . Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a target of doubling exports to countries other than the U.S. over the next decade . China, which is already Canada’s second-largest trading partner, with about $125 billion of two-way merchandise trade in 2025 , is an obvious part of that strategy. But expanding trade with China brings its own risks. Its economy is facing mounting pressures , including a prolonged property-market downturn, a shrinking population and escalating trade tensions with the U.S. For Canada, the question is how resilient that relationship would be if the Chinese economy entered a prolonged slowdown. Could efforts to reduce dependence on one major trading partner leave Canada increasingly reliant on another? Japan’s experience offers a cautionary lesson. As Canada pursues trade diversification, it must be careful not to replace its dependence on the U.S. with a new dependence on China. The warning signs Japan’s economic trajectory offers a striking example of how quickly expectations of continued growth can unravel. In the 1980s, it was widely expected to challenge the U.S. for global economic dominance . Instead, the collapse of its property and stock market bubbles in the early 1990s ushered in decades of stagnation. Land prices fell for 14 straight years , with commercial land dropping to about one-third of the 1991 level . This period became known as Japan’s “lost decades.” China, now the world’s second-largest economy, faces some comparable pressures. Its property market has been in decline since 2021, eroding household wealth and weakening local government finances . Its population has fallen for four straight years , and the government’s 2026 growth target of 4.5 to five per cent is its lowest since 1991 . China is also facing escalating trade tensions with Washington. Restrictions on Chinese exports and access to advanced technologies have intensified the economic rivalry between the two countries. There are, however, important limits to the comparison. China’s economic structure, political system and global position are different from Japan’s. But Japan’s experience shows why Canada should weigh the risks before becoming overly reliant on another major trading partner. Why China is different Several key differences could send China down another path. Unlike Japan, it has a state-controlled banking system , which gives Beijing greater capacity to absorb losses or delay needed restructuring. China is also poorer and less urbanized than Japan was in 1990, leaving more room for growth in household wealth and domestic consumption. It has so far established leading positions in electric vehicles , batteries and solar panels . Its relationship with Washington is fundamentally different, too. Japan was a U.S. ally, and its trade disputes took place within an established security relationship. China, on the other hand, is a strategic rival that competes with the U.S. for influence. China has a population of 1.4 billion people but this doesn’t automatically translate into strong consumer demand. Household consumption is about 40 per cent of GDP, compared with an OECD average of about 60 per cent . That imbalance has contributed to China’s reliance on exports to sustain its growth. In 2025, net exports accounted for about one-third of its growth, the highest share since 1997 . What a slowdown means for Canada Canadian exports to China are heavily concentrated in commodities, which leaves them particularly exposed to changes in Chinese industrial activity and resource demand. Canadian energy exports rose about 78 per cent in 2025, reaching roughly $9.5 billion as the expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline opened up greater access to overseas markets. But China’s oil demand is weakening , with further declines expected. A prolonged slowdown could accelerate that trend, reducing demand for Canadian energy and putting downward pressure on global commodity prices. Other Canadian exports are exposed to China’s property downturn. Steelmaking coal, copper and lumber, are the most tied to construction and infrastructure investment, so a prolonged contraction in the property sector would weaken demand for these materials. The geographic concentration of Canadian exports adds to the risk. Alberta and British Columbia accounted for 92 per cent of the recent growth in exports to China . Both provinces have substantial resource sectors and are particularly exposed to changes in Chinese commodity demand. Interdependence is not the same as trust Economic ties cannot be separated from political and security relationships. When trade is concentrated, governments can use access to supplies or export markets as leverage in disputes. During the trade disputes of the 1980s, Washington pressured Tokyo to open its markets. Japanese carmakers such as Honda and Toyota built plants across North America, including in Ontario , creating jobs and embedding Japanese investment in North America. The pattern continued under U.S. President Donald Trump. In 2025, Japan pledged US$550 billion in American investment as part of an agreement to resolve tariff disputes. In both cases, a longstanding political and security alliance provided a foundation for negotiating trade disagreements. Japan’s relationship with China offers a different lesson. During a territorial dispute in 2010, Japanese businesses reported Chinese shipments of rare earth minerals had stopped . This incident exposed Japan’s dependence on China for materials, and Japan subsequently worked to diversify its supply, cutting China’s share of its rare earth imports from about 90 per cent to 60-70 per cent . Canada has encountered a similar vulnerability. After imposing 100 per cent tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 , China responded with tariffs on canola. Exports to China subsequently fell 62 per cent . A deal reached in January lowered canola tariffs in exchange for allowing 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles into Canada annually at a 6.1 per cent tariff. Lessons for Canada Japan’s experience highlights two lessons in Canada’s push to diversify trade. The first is that an economic slowdown does not necessarily make a country an insignificant trading partner. Japan remained a wealthy and important market long after its property bubble burst. China, however, could face prolonged stagnation before reaching Japan’s level of affluence. If Chinese demand weakens, commodities producers will have to compete for a smaller pool of buyers. The second lesson is that the political relationship behind trade can matter as much as trade volume. Japan’s ties with the U.S. survived disputes partly because they ran both ways: Japanese firms built plants in North America, and the two countries shared security interests. Japan’s dependence on China demonstrated the risks of relying too heavily on a single source of important resources. Canada’s relationship with China is more asymmetric. Much of the trade involves Canadian commodities flowing one way, with market access Beijing can grant or withdraw. Trading dependence on Washington for dependence on Beijing would simply replace one vulnerability with another. Canada’s priority should be to expand its customer base. Its Pacific coast can ship crude, gas and critical minerals to Asia, while the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership gives Canada preferential access to Japan and other Indo-Pacific markets. Trading with more countries is not the same as having more freedom to choose. The goal is to ensure that no single partner — whether rival or ally — can set the terms. Amir Bahman Radnejad is affiliated with Canadian Global Affair Institute. Masaru Karube is affiliated with the Institute of Innovation Research, Hitotsubashi University, Japan.

articles.content: Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced a plan in the 2026 federal budget aimed at eliminating homelessness in the next decade. A statement about the plan says homelessness “strikes at the heart of Canadian values of fairness, solidarity, and human dignity.” What are these values and how exactly are they impacted by homelessness? The announcement does not clearly answer these questions. As a researcher in public health ethics, I want to fill the gaps by drawing on empirical and philosophical research to explain why, exactly, the urgent need to address homelessness is matter of ethics. Eroding dignity Dignity refers to a kind of inherent worth that all people hold equally by virtue of being human. It serves as the foundation for human rights, which provide people with entitlements and establish obligations for others (including governments) to treat people in ways that respect their rights. Violations of those human rights , which include a guarantee to adequate housing , are one way people experience a loss of dignity when homeless. Some policy responses to homeless encampments have also violated rights guaranteed under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and therefore peoples’ dignity . Homelessness violates dignity in other ways. A lack of shelter, housing and a home — understood as a place of belonging — leads people to experience shame and ostracism. Homelessness excludes people from meaningful participation in social life. That leaves them on the margins of society, with little to no resources or options, reduced social status and a lack of freedom and authority over their lives since much of what they do, even just to survive, is criminalized . In these ways, homelessness reduces people to being less-than, unworthy, and unequal. What makes a just society? This brings us to fairness and related questions about what a just society looks like. In one view , a just society involves how people stand in terms of equality with one another rather than in hierarchic relations. The failure of the state to adequately respond to homelessness is a profound injustice because it demonstrates a lack of equal concern for some of the most vulnerable members of society. And, as some argue , this is precisely what’s at play in terms of homelessness. Another famous view comes from American philosopher John Rawls . For him, justice as fairness is concerned with the distribution of benefits and burdens in society, according to two principles . The first principle states that everyone has an equal claim to basic liberties. The relevant part of the second principle, called the difference principle, holds that any social and economic inequalities in a just society should give the greatest benefit to the least advantaged members of society. Although this view tolerates some inequality, homelessness remains incompatible with its principles of justice. Rawls didn’t name housing as one of the benefits to be distributed under these principles. Some scholars have argued that it must be one of the social goods we should be concerned about distributing fairly, through, say, social housing models. The fact that homelessness exists to the degree it does in a wealthy country like Canada does in fact suggest a lack of fairness in a broader distributive sense. Some people are left without shelter altogether, some have subpar shelter while others have plenty. But the causes of homelessness are complex and multi-faceted . The problem has been made worse by a lack of affordable housing, higher unemployment and overall higher costs of living associated with rising inflation. In research on the causes, experts and advocates agree that it’s not caused by the choices people make, but the choices we make as a society . Health inequities Such social choices have ripple effects, as people who experience homelessness face risks to their health and well-being. Homelessness disproportionately affects some populations , which can lead to vicious cycles of poor health, higher risk of infectious disease and premature death . Homelessness therefore leads to inequities in health. Homelessness is an affront to human dignity, and it’s unfair. The concept of solidarity speaks to the need for society generally to address injustices as a collective. Failing to do so results in the social and moral abandonment of people experiencing homelessness as they are left to suffer the injustices of homelessness alone. While these arguments make a compelling ethical case for ending homelessness, the real work lies in translating justification into action. In addition to monitoring and evaluating the practical outcomes of the promised federal funds, Canadians should not lose sight of the ethical values underpinning them and the overarching goal of ending homelessness. We need to ensure our policies not only reflect our ethical values, but also produce outcomes that actively support them. We must consider whether the policies and programs implemented align with our ethical values, and whether their outcomes are effective in promoting them as well. Nicole Fice has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council for a project on the ethics of encampment evictions.
